I would like to inquire from the government whether or not any report has yet been received from the commissioners who were appointed to investigate certain matters in connection with) the Tneadgold and other concessions in the Yukon ? If the report has not been received, I would like to inquire whether or not the evidence has been received, and in either case I would like to know the intention of the government as to printing that evidence in full.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS Hon. James Sutherland). The right hon. the Prime Minister is not at present in the House, but I will mention the matter to him, and my hon. friend might renew his question when he is present.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL (Hon. Sir William Mulock) moved that the House go again into Committee of Supply.
['Continuation of supplies.']

Before the House goes into Committee of Supply, I desire to call the attention of the hon. the Postmaster General to the very unsatisfactory condition of affairs at Picton post office. The mails for Picton are delivered from the (Grand Trunk Railway over the Central Ontario Railway. The trains over this railway arrive very irregularly, and in consequence the mails are not delivered in the post office until long after the proper hour. The railway company carries the mail on the same train that they use for shunting and handling all the freight at the stations along the line, so that its arrival at Picton is very irregular. While the railway company is largely to blame, the staff of the post office is also highly inefficient, and the time occupied by them in the sorting and distribution of the mails is utterly unreasonable. In fact the staff has never been an efficient staff. The postmaster has had no clerical training and the hands in the office have been boys, also without training. With the exception of one young mail named Belch, there has never been a really efficient or competent official in that post office under this (Government. I hope the Postmaster General will find means to remedy this evil,

which is a cause of inconvenience to all of the inhabitants of Picton. Mails which should be delivered at 9 a.m. o'clock, or 9.30 a.m. at the outside, are frequently not delivered until 11 o'clock, and a similar state of affairs exists in the afternoon.

I am sorry to learn from my hon. friend (Mr. Alcorn) that any cause for complaint exists, and I will take all possible means to remedy any evil. As to the first portion of the hon. gentleman's complaint, that mail trains are used for handling local freight as well as for handling passengers, I fear the remedy is beyond the control of the government. As to any inefficiency on the part of the post office staff, that is a matter for which the government is responsible, and if this condition should continue it would be a ground of complaint against the government. Therefore, I assure my hon. friend that any ground of complaint of that kind will cease at the earliest possible moment. As to the former ground of complaint, I will bring that matter to the attention of the railway in question and ascertain whether it would be possible for them to improve their methods.

I wish for .a few minutes to allude to a question on which some difference of opinion occurred in the House the other day, and which I think it is desirable to have cleared up. I refer to the differences of opinion between the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) and the right hon. Prime Minister and myself with reference to the bonding privilege and coasting laws as exercised by the United States. It will be remembered that the Prime Minister thought that goods could not be shipped from one point or place in the United States to another American port or place except in American vessels. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) thought he was wrong in that, and that it might be shipped in Canadian vessels as well as in American vessels. On that occasion I read the law of the United States, which is:	.
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled: That no merchandise shall be transported by water under penalty of forfeiture thereof from one part of the United States either directly or via a foreign port or for any part of the voyage in any other vessel than a vessel of the United States.
The leader of the opposition on that occasion said it would depend upon what interpretation might be put upon the word ' voyage,' and asked if there had been any decisions of the Supreme Court in that ease. I said I was not aware, that the commissioner of the department was looking to see. Well, the commissioner has not been able to find any decisions. But we have here Mr. ALCORN.
the customs regulations of the United States, the instructions given to their officers by the Treasury Department, which they are to carry out in this respect, and they are set forth in article 707 :
Merchandise in transit from one port or place within the territory of the United States to another by a route a part of which is by land carriage through the Dominion of Canada, and a part by the great lakes and the rivers connecting the same, or by the River St. Lawrence, may be transported by water in American vessels only from ports on the northern frontier of the United States to ports on the Canadian frontier for transhipment to railway cars, from points on the Canadian frontier at the termini of railway transportation, to ports on the northern frontier of the United States.
It is as the Customs Departmeut thought, and as the Prime Minister thought; it is absolutely forbidden by tbeir statute as interpreted by their customs regulations, to carry goods otherwise than in American vessels from one American port to another. However, while the department felt sure, it did not like to speak too positively, and we thought we would find out positively how this matter stood, and for that reason the Commissioner of Customs wired Mr. Drewitt, who is Canadian Customs Officer at Depot Harbour, ou October 1st, 1903 :
Regarding freight originating in Boston destined for Duluth, carried by railway to Depot Harbour, will American officer allow this to be carried from Depot Harbour to Duluth in British vessel, wire reply.
The reply is as follows :
Depot Harbour, Ont., October, 1903. To John McDougald,
Commissioner of Customs,
Ottawa.
American customs officer will not allow freight originating in Boston destined for Duluth to be carried in British vessels from Depot Harbour to Duluth.
(Sgd.) F. J. DREWITT.
While that has reference to package freight, we wanted to be sure. It was suggested then that they might allow it to be carried for export, that grain originating at Duluth or Chicago might be sent to Liverpool via Boston. I said at the time that I did mot think that could be done. But I did not wisli to speak too positively, and in order to find out that point positively, the commissioner, on the 1st of October, wired Mr. Drewitt, the customs officer at Depot Harbour, Ontario, as follows :
Regarding American wheat from Duluth to Liverpool transported by railway from Depot Harbour to Boston, will American officer allow this wheat to be carried in British vessel from Duluth to Depot Harbour ? Wire reply.
This is the reply :	.
Depot. Harbour, October, 1903.
To John McDougald.
Commissioner of Customs,
Ottawa.
American customs officer will not allow American wheat from Duluth consigned to Liverpool

[DOT]via Depot Harbour and Boston to be carried on other than American vessels.
(Sgd.) F. J. DREWITT,
Customs Officer.
Now, I tliinlc that places the question in such a clear light before the House, that there can be no further doubt, and I have read these telegrams thinking they might be useful to the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS (Hon. William Paterson).

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has made a portion of that matter fairly clear, but there is one aspect of it which he has not made clearer than it was before, and as to which I do not think his references have any application. It is perfectly clear, .notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman has said that we can bring grain or any other freight capable of being stored in an elevator, from Duluth or Chicago to Depot Harbour, consigned to Depot Harbour,
- and store it in an elevator there; then, after it has been so stored, we can route it thence either by Boston or by any port in Canada. But I would like to point out to the Minister of Customs that what the right hon. gentleman said in the course of the debate to which he has made reference, is something very different from that which the Minister of Customs has placed before the House to-day. Here is the language of the right hon. gentleman to be found on pages 12647 and 12648 of 'Hansard':
We would have to manag a fleet of steamers. There is something more. The fleet maintained on the lakes for the purpose of supplying traffic to the' Canada Atlantic Railway is composed in part of American bottoms. It would be impossible to have the trade we have to-day unless it was carried in American bottoms. We can carry Canadian freight in Canadian bottoms, but you cannot take freight at Duluth, Chicago or Milwaukee or any of the western ports and bring it to Depot Harbour except in American bottoms.
The PRIME MINISTER Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier). That was qualified.
The right hon. gentleman did not qualify it at all. I am reading his own language.
That is not all.

I will read it all :
The bonding privilege of the Americans has been so devised as to make that a necessity. Therefore the Canadian government would have to become the owners of a fleet of steamers under American register.
It is perfectly obvious, not only from the fact that the right hon. gentleman did not qualify his language, but from another circumstance, that he was under that impression at the time; because we were not proposing to acquire the Canada Atlantic Railway or any other extension of the Intercolonial to the Georgian bay for the purpose of taking freight to Boston, we were proposing to acquire that railway for the purpose of taking freight to Halifax,
and St. John, and Quebec, and Montreal. That is what my right hon. friend was dealing with, if he was dealing with anything. Nothing could be more absolute, nothing could be more unqualified than his language which I have just read. The right hon. gentleman was dealing with a railway which, we will say, transports a considerable portion of grain from Duluth and Chicago to Depot Harbour. That grain, so far as I am aware, is carried principally if not altogether from Canadian ports. I asked my right hon. friend the other day whether he was aware that any considerable portion of this grain was exported from United States ports-I am referring to grain brought to Depot Harbour and carried by the Canada Atlantic Railway to Montreal. My right hon. friend was not able to say that any considerable portion of that grain did go by American ports. What w'e were dealing with was bringing American grain to Depot Harbour and transporting that grain to Europe via Canadian ports. My right hon. friend obviously was of the opinion that that could not be done, otherwise he would not have used the absolute and unqualified language which he did use with regard to that matter.

I have only one word to say. I cannot find at this moment my language, but I am satisfied that if my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will look again and see what I said, he will find that I stated that the traffic of the Canada Atlantic Railway was American traffic passing from American ports to American ports and that that traffic could not be carried on the lake except in American bottoms to be bonded on the Canada Atlantic Railway. That is the statement which I made at the time, certainly which I intended to make and I am pretty sure that I did so in so many words in some part of the remarks which I made.

My right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) stated that two days afterwards in reply to a question put to him, but I do not think he stated it at that time. May I be permitted to bring another matter to the attention of the gov* ernment, and it is the very negligent and careless way in which the returns have been brought down in compliance with an address of the House of Commons dated the 11th of May, 1903. I moved on that date for copies of all Orders in Council, memorials, letters, telegrams and other correspondence relating to the granting of provincial autonomy to the Nortlh-w,est Territories. On the 19th of June, I directed the attention of the government to the fact that these documents had not been brought down. On the 26th of June my right hon. friend the Prime Minister brought down certain documents and said that there were some more to follow. On the 29th of June I moved that these documents should be printed. On the

20tli of July, after having examined these documents which had been brought down, I spoke of this return and pointed out a very long list of documents which I had been at great pains to tabulate, and which had not been included in the return brought down. Some of the documents which had been omitted were of the most important character. My right lion, friend said that these further documents would be brought down. On a subsequent occasion the lion. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) made a request for the postponement of the discussion of certain financial questions touching the North-west Territories to which I agreed. This was on the same day, the 20th July, and I suggested that the documents should be put in chronological order and should be printed. On the 24th July the hon. Minister of the Interior brought down a further return. I pointed out to him once more that a number of documents which were of very great importance had not been included in the former return. He stated that certain of these documents could not be found, and I offered to supply copies of the documents which could not be found, because I had obtained them from the printed proceedings of the North-west Territories. The first return which was brought down is printed as Sessional Paper No. 110, and the second return is printed as Sessional Paper No. 116a. These returns are still imperfect as a very large number of letters have been omitted and particularly two letters of very great importance, one from the right hon. Prime Minister to Mr. Haultain dated the 8th of June, 1903, and Mr. Haultain's reply dated 15th June, 1903. Besides those I believe from the very hasty examination of the return that a very considerable number of other letters to which I called the attention of the government have not yet been brought down. I do not know whether they are of great importance or not because I have not had time to go over the matter again. I spent half a day in July in going over the documents, and I gave a long list of the letters which were required and which will be found at pages 6891-2 of the revised ' Hansard.' The right hon. gentleman will find that I gave a list of between thirty and forty letters that have not been included in the first return brought down. I do not know whether it would be possible at this period of the session to bring down these documents and have them printed. I do think a little more care should be exercised in regard to these matters. I know there was some difficulty because a certain portion of the correspondence was in the Department of the Interior, and a certain other portion was in the hands of the right hon. Prime Minister. The return which lias been brought down is in a most embarrassing condition. You look for a letter of June, 1901, and you find it at the end of Sessional Paper No. 116a, the second return, while Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
you find another letter of a subsequent date at the beginning of the first return. The letters seem to have been thrown together in a confused heap and printed just as they were brought down. To place these important documents before the House in that way is of no assistance to any member of this House who desires to understand the position of affairs as disclosed by this correspondence. If there is not enough clerical assistance in the service of the government or in the service of this House to see that the returns are put in proper order, 1 think we had better make a sufficient appropriation to provide for that work. I would be ashamed as far as any work in my own business is concerned, and I think any corporation would be ashamed to have documents brought down in so irregular and confused a condition for the purpose of dismissing a business question of any kind, and why we should have to submit to this in connection with the public business is more than I can understand. It is not for want of attention on my part, because I spent nearly a whole day some time before the 20th of July for the purpose of ascertaining what documents had not Ibeen brought down and of suggesting to the government the importance of having these documents brought down in an orderly arrangement. I trust that when documents of great importance are brought down in the future there will be some attention given to the work of having them arranged in chronological order. It would not be out of place where documents are somewhat voluminous to have the return accompanied by an index and to have the printed return accompanied by an index, so that we could readily get at any document that we require. But really a great waste of time is imposed upon those members who desire to study documents brought down in this manner and there must be an absolutely unnecessary waste of time under the circumstances of this case.

There are two documents which perhaps my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) would like to have ; those are the letter of myself to Mr. Haul-tain of the 8th of June, and the answer of Mr. Haultain of the 15th of June. I can bring these down this very day. In regard to the remarks made by my hon. friend, I must admit that the returns are brought down in a very slovenly manner. I shall give directions at once that an officer shall be appointed whose duty it shall be be to prepare all documents properly for presentation to this House. In former years I had often to complain of this matter. I am very sorry that we have not made very much improvement in this regard. I agree with what my hon. friend has said.
If I may be permitted to revert to the subject which was mentioned a moment ago, I would call my hon. friend's attention to page 12*147 of ' Hansard,' where he will find the remark that I made :

I come now to the main proposition of my hon. friend. He proposes to acquire the Canada Atlantic Railway as it exists to-day. But though the government may acquire the Canada Atlantic Railway, it certainly could not operate it. How could you expect that a Canadian government could possibly, with any advantage to the country operate the Canada Atlantic Railway. It is within the knowledge of everybody that at this moment three-fourths at least of the business of the Canadian Pacific Railway and three-fourths of the business of the Canada Atlantic Railway is American business. It is business connected with the western states and carried to its destination in the eastern states. The Canadian government could not compete for that business if we were to acquire that railway.
Then I proceeded to give the reasons.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Abbott's Harbour, N.S., $700.
This is to build an addition to the beach protection 30 feet in length. This is the amount estimated to complete the work.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: What county is it in ?
Yarmouth.
Would the minister be good enough to state what county each work is in V

And the object of the expenditure in each case.
Abram's river-wharf, $1,000.

This is for rebuilding a small stone wharf in Yarmouth county which was built 25 years ago. This is the total amount estimated by the chief engineer. These repairs will be done under the supervision of the engineer in charge.
Who fixes the wages when it is done toy day labour ?
The engineer in charge.
Does the fair-wage officer interfere in any way V
I suppose he would if there was any complaint, but we have never had complaint.

I suppose the fair-wage officer is held in reserve in case of emergency.
Bayfield harbour works-repairs and improvement, $6,850.
This is .in Antigonish county, and this sum is the total estimated cost.
Is there any considerable commerce at Bayfield, or is this for the benefit of the fishermen?

This is a very important harbour. To show how important it is, I
may say that the Conservative government in 1889, voted $3,500 to commence the building of a wharf, and between 18S9 and 189G they expended $40,000 on this wharf.
Is not that enough ?

Since the Liberals came to power only $1,000 has been expended. This present expenditure has been reported by the engineer to be urgent, in order to keep tlie work from going to decay. There was a breakwater built by the Conservative government, and there has been since no expenditure on that work until now. The engineer lias reported that the whole covering has been swept away by the storm last year, and it is to rebuild the covering of the breakwater that the sum is necessary.
Will the vote be sufficient ?
So the engineer reports.
Is there any considerable commerce at this point ?

Before the building of the Intercolonial Railway to the strait of Canso, it was the most important shipping place in the county, and although it is not so -important now, still there is considerable business done in the shipping of cattle to Newfoundland. As Antigonish is almost entirely a farming county, that is an important" industry with us. During the summer, two or three vessels make fortnightly trips between Bayfield and St. John's, Newfoundland. It is the chief port for Newfoundland vessels.
How will this money be expended V
It is practically for repairs, and it will be done under the supervision of the government engineer.

Is Mr. Dod-well the engineer 7
The MINISTER OI<' PUBLIC WORKS. Mr. Milledge is in charge.
How many resident engineers are there in Nova Scotia ?
There are two, Mr. Dodwell and Mr. Mill-edge.
I think Mr. Locke has jurisdiction in the western part of the province.
Yes, there are three altogether.

Does the minister think that there is necessity for three resident engineers for that province-there may be ; I am only asking for information ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, The chief engineer says he should have more. Now that the matter has been brought to my attention, I will inquire into

it at an early date. I can understand that when a lot of money is being expended at different places it would be a saving to the country to have a responsible man in charge.
Baxter's Harbour-reconstruction of breakwater. $2,000.

This is in King's county. It will cost $3,000 to reconstruct the work, and put it in good shape. There is considerable local trade from fishermen and farmers in that district. The money will be expended under the supervision of the local engineer. This is practically repairs, and cannot be done by contract because you do not know when you commence how much work you will have to do.
Will this vote cover the total expenditure ?

No, the total cost is $3,000.
Benoit's Cove-improvements to boat landing $800.
This is the total cost of improvements that have been made at this point-the removal of 183 yards of boulders and the placing ot' 183 yards of stonework.
For what purpose is the boat landing used ?

This is for the benefit of a large fishing district. There has never been a wharf on the east side of Harbour Bouche. Altholigh there are forty or fifty large boats engaged every year in the fishing industry in that part of the harbour, there is no protection whatever for them. Benoit's Cove affords splendid natural protection for boats except for a number of boulders which obstruct the navigation. An investigation was made by the resident engineer last year, and he has reported that by the removal of these boulders very safe and secure shelter would be afforded to the fishermen in that locality.
Big Harbour (Port Bevis)-wharf, $3,700.
This is to cover the cost of building a wharf 80 feet long and 12 feet deep at low water on the west side of the harbour. It is in Victoria county, N.S.
Is this a new wharf ?
Yes, this is a new work, and this $3,700 is the total cost estimated by the engineer.

I am not going to find fault. I merely wish to say that there is a disposition to extend works in many cases and to build new works, which no doubt the people of the localities served may not object to ; but the question is whether they are of a character so pressing that they should be undertaken. These works not Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
only involve present expenditure, but they become a public charge for all time. Our experience under all governments has been that once you construct the most useless work, the people of the locality will never listen to the suggestion that an end should be put to it, though they know it is useless. I am not sure that the governments of the day are inclined to turn a dellf ear to these demands, especially on the eve of elections. Only a short time ago the Minister of Labour, Postmaster General and acting Minister of Public Works-I do not know that that trinity exists now-sent out a circular inviting applications for works, I presume, of this kind. I would like to ask the present Minister of Public Works if this work is the result of that invitation, or if it is a work of absolute necessity. While I am not prepared to say that it is not a necessary work, because I have no information' on the subject, I do say that this committee should scrutinize with great care any expenditure of this character, unless it is shown to be of some importance and of some lasting benefit. Will the hon. minister give us some statement as to the necessity of this, and what the engineer reports.

The representation made to the department is that the farmers and other inhabitants of that district can only dispose of their produce by taking it to Baddeck, a distance of nine or ten miles, and that this small work will give them accommodation by water.
What is the report of the engineer ?
I am reading now from the report of the engineer.
When was that report made ?
On the 14th of April last.
How many people are tributary to that part ? What is the nature of the country around ?

As one who knows a little about the district, I may say to my hon. friend that this is not a useless work by any means. The community that is to be served by this wharf is a rather important community. It is a good farming district, and there is considerable fishing besides. The people live in a part of the country which is not served by a railway, and there is no likelihood that there will be a railway in the near future. Their only means of communication is by water. I repeat that it is not by any means a useless work, but is a necessity to accommodate the farmers and fishermen of the district.
Can the minister tell the committee how near this harbour is to other harbours 7
As I have already informed the hon. gentleman-I suppose he is only asking for fun
I want the hon. gentleman to understand that there is no fun about this.

I thought it was for amusement, because I have already within five minutes stated twice that at present the people have to haul their produce to Baddeck, which is nine or ten miles away. I am not able to say how far distant the nearest harbour is.
The nearest harbour is Baddeck.
Might I ask the minister if there is any revenue derived from any of these wharfs ?

When the work is completed by the Public Works Department, it is transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, which collects the revenue. 1 should fancy that the revenue in this particular district would not be very large.
I suppose the question whether there will be any revenue is taken into consideration by the government ? I notice that in these supplementary estimates there are votes for 103 places in Nova Scotia.
There ought to be 203.
That shows the hon. gentleman's idea of public expenditure.
How many harbours are there in Nova Scotia ?
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition said the other day that there were several thousand.
In what county is this wharf located ?
In Victoria. It is to connect the government wharf with the public highway, and the cost is $5,528.29.
Was there any contract ?
The work was let by contract.
When this item was up for discussion last year the minister said that the contract was let and that the work would be completed in June.
My information is that it was completed in June.
The statement was made last year that the vote then taken would complete the work.

The chief engineer informs me that the statement then made was that the vote being taken would complete the work then under contract. The estimate now asked is for the building of a road 2,100 feet long connecting the wharf with the public highway, this being a different work from that to which the hon. gentleman refers.

Might I ask the hon. minister how much money has been expended in the past few years on this work ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIOi WORKS.
I am most happy to repeat again that the amount is $5,520.29.

The $4,000 voted last year was the first investment in that wharf and this is an item to complete it, making the total cost over $5,000 ? Does the hon. gentleman expect there will be any revenue from this ?	.
I should think there should be some small revenue from this wharf.
Is that roadway a new work ?
Yes.
Was the land on which it is built purchased ?
Yes, the chief engineer informs me it cost $70.

I would like to ask if this is not a new departure, building Wharfs and also highways to connect them. I should think that when the public of Canada contribute money to build a wharf the people of the municipalities might build a road to connect with it.
There is a good deal in what the hon. gentleman says, but it is not a new departure. There is a great deal in what my hon. friend says that localities might do some of this work.

Has the minister considered that by undertaking to build highways which are properly within the control of the' municipalities by virtue of the delegation of control over highways to provincial governments and the municipal authorities, this government may become responsible for the maintenance and repair of these highways and for any accidents that may occur upon them ?
I' suppose that if the work is done on our own property the liability of the government will not be the same as if this was on a public highway.

Would the hon. minister kindly give us some idea of the principle underlying the distribution of this pub-

lie money all along the Nova Scotia coast ? It seems extraordinary that a public wharf is built on the coast where there is no means of access to that wharf.

I may say iu reference to the vote for Nova Scotia generally that these works are certainly required in the public interest. A wharf for example may be required' in a fishing village. The highway runs parallel to the coast and between it and the shore there may be small cultivated pieces of land. The wharf is located at the place where it will best suit the people of the district. There may, however, be no road running down to it and it may be necessary to build a road from the highway to the wharf which may be some little distance.

I would like to know whether a public port must be constructed for every one or two farmers along the coast. It seems to me an extraordinary thing that public money should be squandered in this manner, frittered away-I can only say it is-by building wharfs and places that require to be kept up later by the government, for which there is so little public use that there is no roadway into them at all, and the government have not only to make the wharfs but to build a road to them for the benefit of one or two farmers. If public money is to be squandered in that fashion, and if claims like that are to be set up for one province, why not for every other province ? Why should not wharfs be built along little rivers ? There are rivers running through my county, and lots of places where it would be convenient for the farmers to have a wharf.

Simply for the reason that these wharfs are built on the seaside where they are the only modes of communication the fishermen have. Besides, the sum total for these little wharfs is not equal to one single expenditure made in some of the other provinces. Here is a district, we will say, where 500 fishermen live by the seaside, and the only mode of communication they have with the outer world is by one of these wharfs. When they get the wharf they need a roadway running from it some distance to a highway in the country. The most suitable place is selected' for a wharf, and then in order to get to it or from it you have to have a road. As to one of these wharfs being for only one Mr. ROSAMOND.
or two farmers, I trust the hon. gentleman's intelligence will not allow him to speak in that manner.
Does the hon. member for Guysborough mean to say that the fishermen on that coast have a right to have wharfs all along the coast ? That is an absurdity.

How could a schooner get to land unless there was a wharf to which she could be attached ? If the hon. gentleman understood anything about the lower provinces he would know that wharfs are the only method of communication the fishermen have with the inland. It is not at all like a river in Ontario, it is a coast where storms are frequent and violent.

Does every fisherman require a wharf for himself ? It seems to me an extraordinary proceeding to build wharfs all along the coast for objects of that kind, as if these fishermen were not clever enough to get from the coast inland, or to go to some neighbouring town where there is a wharf already buiit.

I did not raise tills question as to the advisability of building wharfs, I raised a question in connection with the road to the wharf, and there has been no explanation given why we should build roads as well as wharfs. Now where a wharf is necessary I do not object Jo furnish the money. But there is a question in my mind about building such a great number of wharfs-we have built hundreds of wharfs, I think I am safe in saying, since the present government came into power. And I want to remind you, Mr. Chairman, when the Conservatives were in power, how your heart was grieved at seeing the government buying up the people with their own money. I remember how the heart of the Minister of Trade and Commerce used to be grieved, and his righteous soul was vexed from day to day, with the unholy acts of the Tory party, when the people of Ontario were being ' bled white,' as he used to say. Now he is not only willing to sit in a position that he used to say was a sinecure, and that never should have been created, but he remains perfectly silent and is willing tamely to submit to this iniquity being perpetrated year by year to a still greater extent. I know, Mr. Chairman, that you feel grieved about it, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce takes it very coolly, he never says a word against it. He is not only willing to see the constituencies bought up by the building of wharfs with the people's own money, but he is willing to sit by and allow the hard-earned money of the people to be used to build roads down to the wharfs. Now I say that we on this side are willing, as a general thing, to vote money for the erection of wharfs where they are necessary, but we draw the line there, and we say that we should leave to the municipalities or to the

local legislatures the charge of building roads for the public to get to these wharfs. I hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce will come to the rescue of the public exchequer ou these lines, and not allow it to be robbed, not allow the farmers of Ontario to be bled white as he said they used to be in days gone by.

I understand the member for Guysborough (Mr. Eraser) to say that these roads are necessary to connect with highways at some distance from the wharf. I would ask that hon. gentleman in what position that will put this government after it has constructed a road from an existing highway to the wharf. Now the Dominion government, as has been pointed out by my hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane), should build a wharf where it is necessary, but after we have built the wharf for Dominion purposes, in the interest of the whole of Canada, I would like the hon. member fo'r Guysborough to tell us who becomes responsible for keeping up that road to the wharf. I do not care wdietlier the road is short or long. The hon. member for Guysborough says some of these highways are a long distance from the wharf, I presume he means a mile or two away. Now is that connecting road tinder the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature, or of the municipality, or does it remain under the jurisdiction of this parliament, and is the Dominion of Canada responsible for keeping it up, and responsible for all the accidents that may occur upon it ? This involves an important principle, and now is the proper time to discuss it. In what position is the province, is the municipality, is the Dominion government, going to be in regard to liability for accidents as well as for keeping this roadway in repair ? Why should not the municipality build this roadway, expropriate the land for the purpose, and keep control of it ? If a municipality which expropriates the^land and builds the highway in the public interest, thereafter becomes responsible for keeping it up, on the same principle does not the member for Guysborough think that the Dominion government becomes responsible for keeping up a highway that it has constructed 1 Does he not think that the municipality can say :	We did not construct this highway,
you did it yourself, and you must be responsible ? Cases have arisen in the province of Ontario where a municipality being asked to take over the control of a highway have said to the government:	You
must give us a sum of money which, capitalized, will allow us sufficient income to keep this in repair. For instance, we want $50,000 from the Dominion of Canada to furnish us an income with which to keep this highway in repair. I can assure the hon. member for Guysborough that this is not as light a matter as he thinks. There is a wharf, and some distance away there is a public highway, and now the Dominion
of Canada is asked to build a roadway to connect the two. Who is to be responsible for keeping that up ? I want the member for Guysborough to enlighten us on this point, if he can.
I am not a lawyer
The Minister of Justice is a lawyer.

I submit as a layman that the action which we may take under a vote of this kind does not in any way affect municipal rights, or Dominion rights, with regard to our responsibility for highways. That question is not involved at all. My hon. friend from Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) is like my-,self, he does not understand the legal aspects of the question.
You had better let somebody answer who does understand it.

There will be no different responsibility on the part of the Dominion in reference to this property than in reference to any other similar property in the country. The property will belong to the Dominion.

I wish to point out the reckless manner in which the government is voting this public money. The hon. minister stated a few moments ago that the total amount required to construct this wharf would be a little over $5,000. I asked the hon. minister if there had been any revenue from this wharf and he said no, that it was a new work last year. Do I understand the hon. minister correctly in making that statement ? The hon. minister shakes his head. I would be very sorry to misquote him. Perhaps he would make a statement as to whether this was a new wharf commenced last year.
The hon. gentleman is mixing the discussion of this item with that of other votes. I said this wharf was completed in June, 1902.

But I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the first expenditure was the $4,850 voted last year. When we were asked to vote this sum last year the then minister said :
The work is not completed yet and there Is' no revenue from it. It will be completed on June 30th.
The hon. minister said in discussing this vote that $4,850 was the whole sum voted for the wharf. I turned up 'Hansard' of 1901, the session previous, and I find that the minister asked for an appropriation of $1,100, and that when this was given he said :
This will complete the work.
The government came forward and asked for $1,100 and the then minister made the statement that It would complete the work.

On the following year the minister came forward and stated that he had the work under contract and this year the hon. minister says that the amount of the expenditure upon it is $4,850. Now, the hon. minister comes forward and says if you vote this $670 the work will be completed and it may be that we will get some revenue from it. That is the ground of complaint we have on this side of the House. We have the promise of the hon. minister that in no case will he ask for an expenditure until he is prepared to give the committee a proper estimate of the cost of the work. I hope that when this $670 is expended my hon. friend will not come back next year and ask for another vote.
Breton Cove-boat landing, $4,600.
What county is this in ?'
This is in Victoria county. This is to provide a boat landing at Briton's Cove. It is practically a wharf for the fishing industry that is going on at that point.
Is this a new work V
This is a new work.
What is the character of the boats that land there ? What class of people are being served now that were mot served before, and how were they served before ?

1 believe these people unfortunately had to get on shore by clambering on the rock or in any way they could manage it. The desirability of having this work constructed is greater now than in the past, because a lobster factory has been established at this point. Ten regular fishing boats are employed and the industry will give employment to quite a large number of people.
If I correctly understood the hon. gentleman lie said that a packing establishment had been recently established there. How long is it since that was established ?

It was established during the last season and it was enlarged during the present year.
. Mr. CLANCY. Who are the parties interested in it ?
I have no infomation.

How much capital is invested in it ? Is it a very large establishment or a very small one ? If it is a very large establishment there can be no complaint about expending money there and I suppose the hon. gentleman is prepared to give that information. .

I have given all the information I can in Mr. BLAIN.
regard to it. I do not know what amount of capital is required to start an establishment of that kind. They have ten regular boats engaged in the fishing industry. The agricultural pursuits in the district, the fishing industry and the establishment of this factory give employment to a great many men and a large number of fishing boats ?
Are' these large or small fishing boats ?
I am unable to give my hon. friend the size of the boats.
Can the hon. gentleman tell the size of the factory or the amount of business done at that point ?

It seems to me that this is a proposal to spend public money for the benefit of that company or individual who has established this lobster factory. Is there any authority for the government spending public money to benefit private individuals ?

It is very difficult to pass any legislation here that does not more directly affect one citizen than another. Even our tariff legislation has sometimes that effect. This expenditure is for the agriculturists and fishermen of the county, and while this factory may benefit, there is no doubt that the people of the locality will reap the greatest benefit from this work.
How far is this harbour from the nearest place of refuge which fishermen might use ?

What is the name of that nearest point ?
The MINISTER t)F PUBLIC WORKS. Ste. Anne's, in Antigonisli county. This is in Victoria county.
Will the minister read the salient points of the engineer's rexiort on this work ?

The report says that this is in Victoria county, on what is called the north shore, the residents being engaged in agriculture and fishing. Some of them fish off the shore near their homes, and others at French river, which is quite a distance.
Who is that report signed by ?
Mr. Milledge reports to the chief engineer, who is responsible to me. There is a lobster factory employing ten regular boats and buying fish from others. I suppose these are the salient points.
Did the engineer report on the number of men employed in the lobster factory, or the magnitude of the business ?
Perhaps, as an engineer, he -would hardly be expected to report on these things. I understand that the extent of a lobster factory is judged by the number of boats more than by the capital invested.

While the engineer might not be expected to report on these things, yet the minister ought to be in possession of information to justify expenditure on this harbour. The minister does not know the value of the output of this factory, and he does not even know who the owners are. The minister has a great many items before him, and it -would be just as well that the committee would look with some anxiety for information regarding these very large expenditures.
How far is this cove from Livingstone's Cove, in the same county ?
Is Livingstone's Cove in the same county ?

I cannot find from the map that it is.

I do not think that any lion, gentleman in this House would object to giving reasonable accommodation for the boats of the fishing population in the province of Nova Scotia, or in the province of Quebec, or in the province of New' Brunswick, or elsewhere in Canada. The difficulty about these appropriations is that they do not seem to be brought before the House upon any definite principle, and that they are brought down with a very considerable lack of the information which the minister should supply. We could get along a great deal better in committee if the minister would give the House all the information which we eventually do elicit by asking a great number of questions. The minister will recognize that in these supplementary estimates, he is asking for an enormous number of appropriations for harbours and rivers in the different provinces, and when such appropriations are brought down in the closing days of the session, it is the duty of the opposition to try to get some information about each item, in order that they may understand how that item can Jie justified in the public interest. So far as our fishing industry is concerned, I doubt very much whether even all the members from the maritime provinces realize the very great importance of our fisheries to the people, not only of the maritime provinces, but to the people of all Canada. So far as my limited re-412
search has gone, it would lead me to believe that we have perhaps not kept pace with modern methods in the development of the fishing industry, such as obtain in other countries. We pursue, to a certain extent, the methods of fifty or .sixty years ago, and those who have made themselves acquainted with the latest appliances for catching and curing fish have assured me that our methods might be very much improved with great advantage, not only to the fishermen of the maritime provinces, but to the people of Ontario and Quebec, who at present are not supplied as they might be with the splendid fish which swarm around our eastern coasts. Let my hon. friends from Ontario and Quebec realize that it is within the bounds of possibility that in a very few years they can have a daily supply of the very best fish in the world from the maritime provinces.
There is no reason why they should not have it. But let them also remember that in order to ensure that supply, we must have in the first place better means of communication between the upper provinces and the maritime provinces. We must bring the fish along more expeditiously. In the next place, let them remember that in order to build up a trade of that kind, it is absolutely necessary that there should be a constant, regular and abundant supply of fish to the merchants who engage in that trade. That is an absolute requisite. Nobody can undertake to supply the needs of a great city like Montreal or Toronto, unless there are fishermen around the coasts on whom he can depend for a regular and abundant supply of fish every day in the week. And in order that there should be that regular supply, there should be a large number of fishermen engaged in the industry, and these in turn must be afforded the necessary facilities for sheltering their boats. In that way this expenditure can be justified, if it is justified at all. It should be made, however, upon some principle, some plan or some system. But, granting all that, granting that it is not made for political purposes, granting that it is not made in the interest of a political party in one district or another, I do not think we should object to it, although I concur in the view that on all occasions of this kind we should have the very fullest information from the hon. gentleman who is presenting these estimates to the House. Around the shores of Nova Scotia there are not only abundant supplies of the fish with which we are all familiar, but by adopting modern methods of fishing, I believe we may find there many other varieties of fish which are used for food in other countries, and which, if they could be supplied abundantly, regularly and constantly, could be sent from Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and even to the west. We have done a good deal in this country to encourage



other industries. We have provided bounties for manufacturing industries; we have regulated our taritf so that these industries should be developed; we have done a good deal for the farming community in the way of providing experimental farms and bringing experts into the country to teach the farmers how to mate butter and cheese and how to utilize their dairy products. But it seems to me that up to this time we have not devoted the attention to the fishing industry which the importance of that great industry demands; and for my part I am prepared to support the government in dealing with this matter on a fair, comprehensive, systematic basis not only by providing the fishermen with adequate accommodation but by giving them assistance in improving their methods of catching and curing fish, and especially by improving the means of transportation, by which the magnificent products of the sea, which are swarming around all the coasts of the maritime provinces, could be brought into the homes of the people of Ontario and Quebec. I assure my hon. friends from Ontario and Quebec-I need not assure the members from the maritime provinces-that in seeking to develop this great fishing industry, we would not be spending public money unwisely. I believe that we have in the fishing industry of Canada, referring more especially to the fishing industry of the maritime provinces, one of the greatest sources of wealth which are the heritage of Canadians at the present time. I do not underrate the magnificent wheat lands of the west or the agricultural resources of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; but the fishing industry of the maritime provinces will, I believe, in the future, if properly developed and sustained, yield in importance to none of these. Therefore, I think It is wise for my hon. friend cue Minister of Public Works to make such of these provisions as are necessary. At the same time, in presenting them to the House, I think it is very desirable that he should show the members from Ontario and Quebec and the west who are not as familiar as some of us from the maritime provinces, with the importance of this great industry, that it is absolutely necessary, in order that the fishermen may furnish a constant, regular and abundant supply, that they should have suitable shelter for their boats not only during the summer season, but also during the winter season ; because I believe the fishing industry can be prosecuted up to a much later date than it is at present. These men who pursue their labours around the coasts often in tempestuous weather, have sometimes almost at a moment's notice to seek refuge In some harbour. I am sure that what I have said here to-day with regard to the Importance of this industry is the view of all my friends from the maritime provinces; and i know that some of them, who have made, this matter much move of a study than I have and who are much more familiar
with the conditions, would be ready and glad to say a word in support of the view's I have endeavoured thus briefly to present to the House.

I am sure that the House must be well pleased with the remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition with regard to the importance of this industry to the Dominion of Canada. I am free to admit that I find in this House and out of it a considerable want of knowledge as to the importance of this industry-an industry which is now bringing to the Dominion treasury a revenue of over $20,000,000 a year; and I am satisfied, from my experience of a year ago, and from the opportunity I have had of looking into the matter, that, with a little assistance and encouragement, the trade could be increased to bringing a revenue to the Dominion of over $40,000,000. I do not make that statement without having given the matter considerable attention. I am pleased that my hon. friend has to-day drawn the attention of the members of this House and the people of the country to the importance of this great industry. As to the point at issue, I will submit to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition whether I have not given satisfactory information in a general way as to the necessity for this work to the fishing industry. My hon. friend has made a very good point, which is not generally understood, namely, that fishermen cannot catch fish wherever they choose to go; but that the fish are to be found only at certain points along the coast, which may be unimportant, so far as population and the presence of other industries. are concerned!, but which may be important places for the fishermen to land their fish. I am sure the hon. gentleman would not expect me, as the minister in charge of this work to give information as to whether it will change the relations between the municipality and the Dominion in regard to the highway. I could not be expected to give the capital invested by the people who established a factory or any details of that kind. In a general way I would be supposed to give information, as for instance the population to be served and the public facilities to be afforded. In that connection the work will be judged on its merits.
How are we to tell its merits unless we know what is the nature and magnitude of the business to be served, the amount of capital to be invested, and why it should not be done by the municipality ?	_

As one having eon-iderable experience in municipal work, I do not see why this government should build roads to public wharfs. If the government expropriate the land and build the road they will be responsible for damages should any occur.
Not if we hand it over to the municipality.

But you are taking it out of the hands of the municipality. When a private company expropriates land and builds a road, it is not the municipality, but the private company which is responsible for damages. If the government were to build the wharf in the constituency I represent for the fishermen, the municipality would be only too glad to build a road leading to it from the highway.
