visitor to the shore sees the bodies of the ' drowned men and hears the wails of their kindred. An understanding of the conditions is essential and it must be understood that these roads connecting the wharf with the highways are exactly what is required to give the people the facilities they need and to aid them in successfully carrying on their business. I hope we will hear no more criticisms from the gentlemen from Ontario whose opposition X am sure results from imperfect knowledge of the conditions.

I wish to say in this connection that I think perhaps we are only beginning to do what must eventually be done. I know there is good reason why the fishing business In Nova Scotia, has not been better aided than it ought to be, and that is because we were expending large sums upon the training of the farmers of this country. That was all right. I was at an exhibition not long ago in the town of Orillia, and I was delighted to find there that at given times all the farmers were called to certain points and there they were taught how to pack apples. A man went through the packing process and gave full explanations. After a little while the wives and daughters were called to another place, and there they were all taught how to make butter by some one who went through the whole process. At another point the farmers' sons and daughters were called together and were taught how to feed poultry, even so small a matter as the best way of killing poultry was not overlooked. Now that was teaching the farmers, and that was all right. Now there are two or three things that must be done in the lower provinces, and everywhere else in Canada where people are fishing, they must be taught the best way of conducting their business. Speaking particularly of Nova Scotia, it is a hard thing for example for men living in a small district to change their methods of putting up fish. The salt fish business particularly is not as well attended to as it ought to be, and I would suggest to the government that one of the best investments they could make would be to have various stations, just as they have in the great province of Ontario, wherever fish packing is carried on, centres where the fishermen could be brought together, and taught the best method of curing salt fish, the amount of salt that ought to be used, and all that ought to be done to put fish up in the best method. We suffer in our fish business particularly when we come in competition with fish that is put up in the old country. There is no people in the world that know how to put up salt fish better than the Scotch. That goes without saying, because they know' how to do everything better than any one else. But when our fish come in contact with the fish put up by people who have been taught with great care the best methods of curing fish, our fish suffer from the

comparison. They are fairly well put up, our fishermen are as intelligent as any fishermen in the world. But if the intelligent farmers of Ontario need assistance and training to conduct their business, it will not be surprising when I say that the fishermen living along the coast, and who follow largely the methods pursued by their fathers and grandfathers, are not able to put up fisli as well as they ought. That is one thing. Now training of that kind would be an excellent thing for them, and 1 am sure there would be no better investment on the part of the government, because every body knows how much fish are put up each year in Nova Scotia. We arc now changing our methods somewhat, and we can sell all the fresh fish, if it is properly put up, that we can catch. I make bold to say that from Halifax down to Louisburg there is the best fishing in the world. Taking Canso as a centre, I think that is' the best fishing district in the whole world.
The second thing the government ought to do is this :	The Intercolonial has beeu^
a little slow in giving facilities for shipment. Now there is one firm in Canso in my own county that pay the Intercolonial nearly $30,000 a year in freight. Well, they cannot get their fish sent off promptly. I have been talking to the department about it, but it takes a long while, as in every department, to get them fully interested. They will furnish a car or two, but if the fish could be got off immediately after they are caught, there is an unlimited market for them in Canada and the United States. The market cannot be too large for the ability of the lower provinces to supply the demand. The ocean is full of fish, they are not decreasing. It takes about thirty-five hours to transport fish from Canso to Ottawa, and we ought to have it carried on express trains, and in that way there is no reason why the whole of Canada could not be supplied with fresh fish within three or four days after they are taken out of the ocean. Now that business can be extended to any extent.
The third thing I would recommend is just what other people are doing. It has been brought to my attention that even in South Africa they have voted quite n large sum to bring a trawler from the old country. That is a thing this government should do. The wonderful thing about the operations of that trawler in South Africa was this, that they discovered fish there thai were never caught before, excellent fish were caught in the deep sea that were before unknown. You must remember that at our present rate and mode of fishing we are only skimming the surface. Of course, when you go out to the banks you get all these, but I am speaking of inshore fishing. Now this government has done a great deal in supplying freezers for the inshore fisheries. and they are now projecting-and I want to thank the government for that-

one or more stations for the bank fishing. The members from Ontario will understand that within the three-mile limit the inshore fisheries are conducted altogether by people who live on the land near by. But the people are becoming wealthier every day, and they are now able to send out schooners 15, 20 or up to 100 miles. In this respect the county represented by my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbacli) takes the lead. They build schooners and send these out on the banks. This year, for example, the people lose between two and three months because they could not get sufficient bait anywhere, and the idea of the government now is to build a large freezer so that vessels from the bank can go in at any time and get their bait. Enough bait can be put up to supply the six or seven hundred vessels in Nova Scotia that are fishing on that bank, a sufficient amount of bait to last the season. Now that is the next move that the government of this country should undertake so far as fishing is concerned. They should undertake to train the fishermen, as they have been doing the farmers, in the best methods of putting up fish ; secondly, they should provide every facility of transportation and of cold-storage, so that immediately the fish are caught they can be put aboard steamers to be taken to the railway stations and carried off in cold-storage. Thirdly, they should find out more about the fish that are in the ocean. I join with my hon. friend from Halifax in saying that after voting this money we have only taken the first step. I speak so far as these estimates are concerned, because the county I represent is not largely interested in the fisheries. We have done a fair share, and I am not complaining. But considering what could be done with this investment in one of our districts ; I know a district where we have now a breakwater, and where men could not get in at all with their boats if there was a storm, they would have to go nine miles to another harbour and stay there all night. My hon. friends from Ontario will understand how pathetic must be the situation of the wives and mothers and sisters of those men who are out all night, and they do not know what has become of them. You will understand the difficulty. The fishermen of Nova Scotia are not coming to this parliament in forma pauperis. It must not be forgotten that the fishermen, man for man, pay more revenue into the treasury than any other class in the Dominion of Canada, for this reason, that they purchase everything that they require, so far as food is concerned, except fish. There they have small pieces of land. I know district after district in which there are men who would be very glad to have as much good land on which to raise vegetables as the space of the floor of this House. Then, it is with very great toil that they take away the stones. I would appeal to
the fair-minded men of Ontario to remember that things have changed and that just as the Nova Scotia fisherman is not able to form an intelligent idea or perhaps give an intelligent vote as to the wants, demands and conditions of the people of the great province of Ontario it takes a long time for a member from Ontario to understand the circumstances of the Nova Scotia fisherman.
I know very well how it strikes a gentleman from Ontario in this House. He says : There are $4,000 0r $5,000 to be expended in Nova Scotia. The first question naturally is :	What are we going to get out of it ?
What) are going to be the receipts ? Why should we make this investment ? I say, as the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Borden) said, that there is more than the simple return. There is the betterment of the whole fishing community, which is made up of a trained and stable population, a population that has a great future, and more than ever from the fact that it possesses the elements of forming a naval contingent such as no part of the world can produce. All these things I am sure will lead hon. gentleman, if they think over the matter a little to come to the conclusion that although the numbers are large the sum total is not. This is not done for political purposes at all. It is done by all governments. It must be under the condition of things and I know that my generous friends from Ontario look upon it in that fight. After enforcing as strongly as I can that view upon the government I would say that the next move should be along the lines that I have indicated. 1 have no hesitation in saying that the muni-ciaplitles should keep up the roads when they are built, perhaps not to the extent that hon. gentlemen propose, but I think I would not find very much fault with the government if they made it a condition precedent that they should do that. But after all, it has been done and I was glad that the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) gave an instance of what had occurred in Ontario. He said that because the government built a road and the municipality were asked to look after it the municipality insisted that they should get a large sum from the government for doing it. The fishing business is of such, a character that it requires even more care than has been given to the agriculturists. The farmer is ten times wealthier than the fisherman. He can see what his neighbour is doing, and he can go to fairs and see what the farmers in other counties are doing. He has a better opportunity than the fisherman for becoming acquainted with the methods of others. If he receives assistance as he should, and I will vote for all reasonable assistance for the agriculturist, the fisherman should get an equal measure if not more assistance from the government. The best way after all is to put the fisherman in a position to produce an article of the highest char-

acter and to put It on the market in the best condition and if that is done it will be found that that money is well expended.

The bon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Fraser) and the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) made an attack upon Ontario as objecting to these expenditures ini Nova Scotia. I entirely deny that we are doing so. I say that Ontario has never objected and will never object to an expenditure that is good for any. particular part of this country and good for the whole country.
I did not attack Ontario. I said that no man coming from Ontario could understand Nova Scotia any more than the man from Nova Scotia could understand the conditions in Ontario.

What I gathered from the remarks of these hon. gentlemen, and I think I was right, was that the Ontario members did not understand the position of Nova Scotia and that they were not just to Nova Scotia or to the fishermen. I resent that assertion or insinuation entirely. I say Ontario will always be and has always been just to Nova Scotia and has never begrudged any expenditure in connection with the fisheries. What we object to is that there is a constant frittering away of money without any definite object in view. I entirely agree with what my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Borden) stated that these fisheries should toe developed and developed upon a system. I have no knowledge of Nova Scotia, but I have a knowledge of the conditions down the St. Lawrence river. For many years I have fished there, and there are no men in this country for whom I have greater respect than the fishermen who live along those shores. They are a fine class of men possessing virtues for which they are to be envied by the people of Ontario or any other part of the country. My own observations from driving along those shores as far down as Ste. Anne des Monts is that as much as 50 per cent of the money which is spent on wharfs is wasted. There has been no system adopted for the proper development of the fishing industry. There has been no systematic endeavour to find out where the wharfs should be placed or how facilities can best be given to the fishermen along the shore. I am quite sure that the same thing holds good in Nova Scotia, and I say that the government in reason cannot spend too much money in developing the fisheries on such lines that the money spent will toe productive. It is not as productive as it ought to be now because of the manner in which it is spent. The fishery industry is a valuable one and may be rendered ten times more valuable than it is to-day if it is properly developed. One illustration is better perhaps than a lot of theories. I was lost year at Matane, which is on the Mr. FRASER.
St. Lawrence thirty miles from the Intercolonial Railway. I was with a party on Friday morning and we caught salmon. We left on Friday, driving to Metis, and we were in Toronto at a quarter past four by the Grand Trunk Railway day express on Saturday, having the fish with us, which were cooked for dinner on Saturday evening, having been caught at Matane on Friday. If that could be done by an ordinary passenger, I claim that with a reasonable amount of investigation, care and judgment by the government, they could give a market for the fish that are caught there that would produce to the fishermen, two, three or four times the return which they get for their fish to-day. What I do complain of is that there is no systematic investigation as to how to spend the money in order to promote the interests of these fishermen and how best to develop the fishing industry, and I claim that as long as we continue to pass item after item for building wharfs here, there and everywhere, without following any systematic plan laid down by men who know their business and who know what is wanted, we are wasting the money of the country and not developing the fishing industry or doing the good to these men that can and should be done.

I was one of those who, like the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier), at one time thought that expenditures for Nova Scotia wharfs that were built were apparently made for party purposes pure and simple, but I want to say iliat I endorse all that my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) has said, and that I believe that a great many of^ the wharfs that are built in the lower provinces are built from necessity.
I can easily understand the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) or any of the members from the lower provinces, advocating the building of a large number of wharfs. I am satisfied that if more members from Ontario had an opportunity of visiting the lower provinces, they would be willing to admit that these items of expenditure are perfectly justifiable. I do not know that it is possible to follow out the suggestion made by the hon. member from Toronto (Mr. Osier), but, as the result of limited observation, my own conviction is that you cannot follow any definite system in the development of the fishing industries of these provinces. It seems to me that the whole province of Nova Scotia is one vast fishing area, and that you have to provide accommodation simply as the immediate necessities of a particular place require at the time being. Personally I endorse these votes for the province of Nova Scotia, believing as I do that they tend to promote the welfare of the great fishing industry of that province.

The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) seems to

know all about Nova Scotia, and I would like to ask biin if the legislature of tbe province has taken any steps to assist the fishing Industry ? Of course, X believe it is the duty of this government to afford harbours of refuge and other accommodation for the fishermen, but tbe legislature of Nova Scotia has been remiss in its duty if it has not given some aid to its fishermen, and the member for Guysborough has been remiss in his duty if he has not insisted on the local government giving that aid.	.
He never dug a fish-worm in his life.	_

Oh, well, I believe he is a fisherman, but that is not. to the point just now. 1 have some knowledge of the farmers of Ontario, and 1 know that they are willing at all times to assist their fellow-countrymen in Nova Scotia, or in any other part of the Dominion. But the farmers of Ontario have been trying to help themselves. They have taxed themselves havily to establish agricultural schools and farmers' institutes, so that the people may better know the science of farming. The people of Nova Scotia should make an effort to help themselves, as the farmers of Ontario have done. I am sure that we in the upper provinces would be only too glad to get this cheap fish from Nova Scotia, and if the member for Guysborough lias not advocated the running of a fish train, lie has not done his duty. It would be far better for him to have a market for Nova Scotia fish in Ontario than to go begging for a market in the United States.

I do not want to be misunderstood. I did not accuse anybody of not helping the fishermen of Nova Scotia. I would like the hou. gentleman (Mr. Robinson) to get more fish from Nova Scotia, because it is productive of very much that he has not got. What I did say was that this government has done a great deal to (educate the farmers of Ontario, and I only suggested that they should do a little to educate the fishermen of Nova Scotia. I think that both the Dominion government and the provincial government should combine to makje the lot of the fishermen as comfortable as possible. That is all I have advocated.

We who come from Ontario would not object to a,ny legitimate expenditure for the fishermen of Nova Scotia, or of any othfer part of Canada. I am surprised that the government supporter from Halifax (Mr. Roche) should venture to assert that the representatives of Ontario are opposed to this expenditure. No cne on this side of the House has objected to one dollar of expenditure for the fishermen of that province. But we do think that the government should be able to give us some idea as to the policy they are pursuing with regard to the expenditure of this
money. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) has told us that the county of Lunenburg is the chief fishing centre in Nova Scotia, but I am surprised in looking over these 103 items that not a dollar is to be expended in that county.
They are engaged in the deep-sea fishing, which is entirely a different thing. They go 500 miles away from home.
But they have to come back to port again.

Is it any wonder that the representatives in this committee would object to this kind of expenditure, which leaves that important fishing county, represented by a gentleman on this side of the House, out in the cold ?
It was well looked after when his friends were in power.

Why, last ^session the hon. member (Mr. Fraser) condemned the hou. member from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) for not getting some money for his county when the Conservatives were in power. Here is a list of 103 votes for Nova Scotia, and the county of Victoria, represented by a government supporter, gets seven of these expenditures to my knowledge, and probably if I knew the topography of the district intimately, I would find that many more of these votes were for that county. I believe that it is a legitimate thing for this parliament to look after the fishermen, but how does it come that so little of this large amount is to be expended in counties represented by Liberal-Conservatives ?
The leader of the opposition does not say so.

The fishermen of Nova Scotia will be grateful to the leader of the opposition for bringing the Liberal members of this House to their feet in defence of their interests. These gentlemen opposite sat quietly by, without uttering a syllable, until the leader of the opposition drew the attention of the House to the facts.

There is no foundation for the statement that these appropriations have been made with any regard to the political allegiance of members who represent these counties. It is true that every county in Nova Scotia is not interested in the fishing industry to the same extent, but the hon. gentleman will find appropriations for works whenever they have been asked for ; I do not know of any appropriation which has been asked for, and which was recommended by the officials of the department, that was not granted. Of course, a great many have had to be overlooked for the present, but the appropriations appear in the estimates irrespective of who represents a particular county.

I will accept the statement of (lie minister, but I will remind him that last session and the session before the hon. member for Lunenburg (Sir. Kaulbach) appealed from his place in this House for an expenditure in his county.
That was in connection with dredging, and not in connection with the fishing industry.

The member for Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) drew attention to the needs of his county in the matter of dredging, but that class of work, is not covered by these items. To the best of my knowledge, the people of Lunenburg have not asked for any appropriation, except in respect to dredging, whicli the hon. member (Mr. Kaulbach) has earnestly pressed here.
Has the county of Lunenburg been taken care of with respect to dredging ?

The vote for dredging is a general vote and does not apply to particular counties. We are at liberty to employ a dredge in any part of Canada where work is needed, and when we can get the dredge. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) laid down the general principle that these votes were for counties represented by friends of the government. I point out to him that there are votes here for the county of Halifax, which is represented by the leader of the opposition.
And also by a government supporter.

There is a vote for the county of Colchester, where there is no government supporter. There are votes respecting the county of Pietou, from which there is no government member. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works calls my attention to the fact that we made a special appropriation for dredging in the county of Lunenburg, and the only reason the work has not been done is that we have not been able to get the dredges. When my hon. friend states that these votes are only given to counties which support the government, he is entirely mistaken. If there are only a few counties in Nova Scotia which send gentlemen to the other side of the House to represent them, that is not our fault; but these moneys have been distributed irrespective of politics ; and, apart from dredging in the harbour of Lunenburg, there was no application for any public work in the county of Lunenburg before these estimates were prepared.

It is very natural that I should offer an expression on a matter of such vast importance as the fishing industry, in which lam very largely interest-Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
ed, coming as I do from the largest fishing county in the Dominion, and being the representative of a class of men who, for bravery and skill, have no superiors. For that reason I am here, and for that reason I am on my feet now to advocate the claims of the fishermen. As last expressions leave the most vivid impressions, I may refer first to the remark which has just fallen from the lips of the hon. gentleman opposite with regard to the county of Lunenburg. I consider that it is right, it is just) it is honest on the part of any government not to discriminate in regard to the distribution of public moneys in the interest of the fishermen ; yet it is a remarkable fact that not one solitary item, so far as I am hware, appears in these estimates for the county of Lunenburg. I must refute the statement that has been made that I have not asked for public benefits for the fishermen. I have asked at every opportunity this session, and have urged their necessity in strong terms. I have asked for a breakwater or pier at Mill Cove, St. Margaret's bay. The Minister of Public Works can find my remarks on that subject, both -this session and last session. I earnestly advocated the claims of the fishermen in that district. They live on an exposed portion of St. Margaret's bay, and are entirely dependent upon the fishing industry for a living. They possess no land from which to -gather any portion of their daily bread, and if their employment or occupation is in any way disturbed, or their rights, uncared for, they must necessarily suffer. I asked for that breakwater in order that they might have their little property, which has cost them many days' toil, protected in the event of storms. Very often these poor men are compelled to leave their homes in the morning before dawn, and perhaps by night they are compelled to take up their anchor and run for shore in, or fearing, a gale. There is perhaps no chance possible of their getting back to their homes till the gale subsides, and as a consequence they are compelled to seek refuge in some other harbour ; whereas a small expenditure would give them a harbour of refuge and protection for their property in the neighbourhood of their own homes. I therefore make the appeal now, and it Is not too late this session to place a sum of money in the supplementary estimates for that purpose. I also asked for the repair of the breakwater at Petite Riviere in my county. This work was started some years ago as a stone structure, which was to have been of lasting benefit ; but it was only partly built when it was allowed to suffer serious injury by the action of the sea in consequence of the laxity of the government in continuing the work, so that a large amount of money has gone to waste. These people depend very largely upon the industry of fishing for their living, and although I made appeals from

time to time on their behalf, I received no favourable response. I ^ ay that the fishermen of the county I represent, more than those of any other county in the Dominion, are entitled to redress, because they contribute more largely than any other county to the revenue. Our fishermen contribute more largely to the revenue of the country than any other class of men, because every article which they require for their daily food, (except a little fish) and their clothing, has to be purchased. When you consider that the fishing industry contributes $20,000,000 yearly to the revenues of the country, I think the county of Lunenburg is certainly entitled to a portion of that revenue. I am here for the purpose of demanding it, and 1 will never refrain from speaking for the rights of the fishermen, feeling satisfied that in so doing I am dojng a God's service. I say that the expenditure should be made indiscriminately in the interest of all the fishermen. If these fishermen, with pride and an intelligent purpose, have returned me ns their representative in the interest of the country, is it fair on the part of the government to treat them in the manner in which they are doing ? I answer for them without any hesitation, certainly not. I say it is not only wrong, but it is unfair and unjust. Now,
I respect the farmers as much as I do any other class of people. We have a bureau of agriculture, which is a sort of school to educate the farmers in the prosecution of their vocation. Why not also have a bureau of fisheries for the benefit of the fishermen, so that they may be taught how to pursue their industry in the most profitable manner ? Fishing has become a seience, and there is no reason why the fisheries on the Atlantic coast should not be developed as well as those in any other part of the world. A few years ago I complained that the farmer was in need of certain redress for wrongs done through the neglect of the government, in not making special inquiry as to the cause of the disappearance of kelp or sea weed.
This product of the sea, the kelp, has not been cared for In a proper manner. Experience had taught the most of our fishermen that the product kelp was destroyed- a sea vegetable matter-in consequence of the over catch of lobsters. I asked on a former occasion that a commission should be sent to the shores of the Atlantic-to my county if the government desired-to ascertain from the fishermen themselves the best method of protecting this sea fertilizer or weed from being completely destroyed. There is a sort of egg or shell fish found on our shores which lobsters feed upon, but in consequence of the depletion . of these waters, of lobsters, those egg or shell fish have become more numerous and a sort of calcareous substance or excrescence or salvia covers the whole bottom of the shores and causes it to be unproductive of
this weed. As a natural result there is no manure of this kind to be found for use as a fertilizer for the farmer. Such results might have been lessened had the government appointed a commission. The farmers are suffering to this day for want of this weed. If we had a bureau of information for fishermen, and a system of correspondence held between the fishermen and the department we would have gained a certain amount of valuable knowledge which would have enabled us to add to the welfare of both the fishermen and the farmers to a great extent. We want a certain distribution of benefits for-the deep sea fishermen. We have along the shores at present-although my county has not availed itself of the privilege of shore freezers for freezing bait in small quantities to supply the shore fishermen. We want as well a supply of bait for the deep sea fishermen. We want the same conditions and the same privileges extended to the deep sea fishermen as are enjoyed by the shore fishermen, which gives them fifty per cent of the entire cost of the construction of freezers, and I think a bonus of $5 for every ton of bait for three years, which is placed in those freezers. If that same benefit were extended to the deep sea fishermen, we would contribute in return a certain amount of benefit to the revenue which otherwise is lost. No doubt the revenue of the country would be greatly benefited this year by the fishermen had they had the benefit of freezers for bait, but the want of that commodify has caused almost a total failure this year of the fisheries in the deep sea. I find that it was not only the fishermen in my own province who have suffered but also the fishermen in Newfoundland. This year in all probability they shall have to come to the rescue of some of the fishermen in order to give them relief. I would not be at all surprised if an appeal should be made to the government, or by others on behalf of these fishermen to enable them to support their families this coming winter. Why should the government be so obdurate, why should they turn a deaf ear to the appeal I am making now on behalf of the fishermen. I am anxious also that the system of fishing should be improved, and if the government would establish a bureau for the fishermen, there would be no difficulty in reaching the desired end, and every one would be benefited. We can have incubators all along our shores for the reproduction of fish. At present a very large amount of the ova or fish egg goes to waste. Why V Because of the lack of care shown by the government. Those incubators, as far as lobsters are concerned, could be placed wherever there are packing establishments or canneries, but I would advocate more strongly that we should use natural ponds where they can be found where the seed lobsters could be placed and where they could deposit their eggs and undergo the natural

process instead of a method that is absolutely artificial.
Is the hon. gentleman not aware that that is being done ?

In one county, Cape Breton; but that is no reason why we should not have one in Lunenburg and other counties. I do not think my hon. friend has gained much comfort by his inquiry. 1 also would advocate the freezing system for the reason that we could utilize those places for the storage of fish and for shipments to the west. That would benefit the fishermen all along our shores from Shelburne to Halifax in the east, and from Cape North to Halifax in the west. By that system they would be able to ship direct by the Intercolonial at Halifax without any interruption to the centre of this Dominion and get in return the products of the west. The farmers in the west and the fishermen in the east would have thereby the beuefit of a larger and more profitable trade. At present we are deprived of that opportunity because we have not the facilities for transportation. Would it not be infinitely better for us to have an amount included in the estimates to enable the fishermen to market their products so that after they have spent their hours, their days, their weeks, their years, their lives in the employment of fishing, they would have a better market for their product than they now have. I would also advocate-although in this perhaps I am in advance of my rights-the granting of a bonus by the government to a specially constructed steamer in order that it might convey bait from these freezers to the banks where the fishermen frequently rendevous and there distribute the bait to those who wish to take it, and also receive the catch of fish and convey them to the freezers. This would be a general benefit. I offer this to the Minister of Public Works merely as a suggestion.
I would suggest that this discussion might be more in order when the estimates of the Marine and Fisheries Department are under discussion.
My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works will remember that I am only commenting on what has been stated by the gentleman who preceded me.

I would not have raised the point except that I think the remarks of the hon. leader of the opposition and the gentleman who followed him were more in reference to the facilities for the transportation and landing of fish.
Mr. DEPUTY SPEAKER, I was loath to interrupt and was waiting patiently until *
the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kaulbaeh) had finished, but then we shall have to adhere more closely to the matter under discussion.

Mr. Chairman, I am much obliged for your kind consideration, but I think it is in the interests of the general public as well as of the fishermen that a public wharf be built on the shores of this Mill Cove harbour. What would be the use of the wharf, if the fishermen had no fish to land and if no boats came to it ? I am dealing with the matter in that way.	Not a dollar is included
in the estimates for Petite Riviere or for Mill Cove, although these places are deserving of a very great deal of consideration and would have had it long ago had it not been for interference. I have asked for a buoy off the eastern entrance to our habour, Lunenburg. This is necessary in the interests of the fishermen as well as for shipping generally, and also for the protection of life and property. Two steamers went ashore at this point within a very short time of each other, and several sailing vessels have been wrecked for want of a buoy; but I have not been able to obtain this necessary article. The constituency I represent pays into the treasury a large amount of money and to be told that we shall not receive one dollar is almost enough to set the people in revolt. I feel that we have not received justice, and it would have been better for the government themselves if they had not discriminated so conspicuously between my constituency and other constituencies, one of which, the constituency of Victoria, has nine votes in the estimates, but where is Lunenburg ? I feel I would be recreant to the trust imposed in me if I remained silent and did not give expression in the most earnest manner to this protest on behalf of the fishermen.
I still trust that the government will come to the rescue of Lunenburg ; it is not too late for them to include items for these purposes in the supplementary estimates that are yet -to cqme down.

The hon. gentleman will excuse me, but I certainly was perfectly in earnest when I said that I did not know that there was an urgent application for. the works he has asked. If the hon. gentleman will let me have a memorandum of the particular one to which he referred, I will have a report on it made at once.
And an amount placed in the supplementary estimates for this year ?
I cannot say that.

It is unfortunate that some of our friends opposite do not know more about Nova Scotia. One gentleman asked if the local government are doing anything for the people. He also said that

they have a school in Ontario. I am sorry that school does not teach more than it does; if it did he would know that the government of Nova Scotia is doing all that it should do for that province and is appropriating about . as much for school purposes as any government in the world. That government also gives the people of Nova Scotia roads and bridges, good iron structures, and before the Dominion of Canada took their revenue they also gave to the people wharfs and piers. It will not do that to-day because the people of Nova Scotia are paying another government to do it. To hear some members talking in this House about the poor fishermen of Nova Scotia you would almost think that they were the recipients of something that did not belong to them. I venture to say that one fisherman in Nova Scotia will contribute to the general revenue of the country as much as half a dozen of your farmers, for the very reason that the fishermen import and buy more of the goods which they consume. I presume that a farmer in Ontario can live largely out of his farm. Our fishermen have to send their fish abroad and get cash in order to buy the produce of Ontario. You will not buy it, and it is a great pity that the people of Ontario will not buy fish-they need it.
Now, what we want from this government is harbours ; let them improve our harbours, improve our piers ; in other words, do for us what we were doing for ourselves before the Dominion government took away our revenue. I think that is very reasonable. When the hon. gentleman across the way was talking of the injustice that was done to his county, I was reminded how often we were told, in the old days, that we could not expect anything from the government, because we were not sending a supporter of the government. That is what we were always -told in the past, and in fact we learned not to look for anything. We did not look ifor anything during eighteen years, because we were taught that we had no right to expect government favours, that this heaven-bom right 'belonged only to those who were supporting the government of that day. Let our friends understand that the fishermen of Nova Scotia are not entirely dependent on the paltry help they may get from this government. The great trouble with our fishermen is that they have not received the attention that the farmer's of Ontario have received. They are scattered over the face of the Atlantic, and they do not often meet together to concoct plans and to send resolutions to the government asking for assistance. It would be well for them perhaps if they did. At the same time, I hope that the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) will travel a little more. He will find that there are schools in Nova Scotia as well as in Ontario. He told us there were schools in Ontario for farming. Well, they might teach their children a little of something else, so that they might
know that there are other places in the world besides Ontario.

The Hon, Finance Minister made the statement that one of the reasons why Lunenburg county was neglected was that the member for that county had failed to put in his requisition for help. I wish to read from the ' Hansard ' of last year a few words of the hon. member for Lunenburg. He said :
I observe quite a number ot estimates for different counties in Nova Scotia. Annapolis appears not to have been overlooked. Neither have Richmond, Guysborough, Victoria, Inverness and other counties. The two counties west and adjoining Lunenburg, not excepted, or in other words, all are included in the roll for benefits. But I am afraid that the Minister of Public Works has forgotten the most important part of the entire coast. He says he is very-desirous of forwarding the interests of the fishermen. ... I may tell him that there is a long stretch of coast in St. Margaret's bay where, for twelve or fifteen miles, there is almost a continuous town, house almost against house for that entire distance, with an immense population. X have been asking for a number of years for a breakwater for Mill Cove, St. Margaret's bay. The property of the fishermen there is in jeopardy every time there is a storm. They have to fish in large boats ; smaller boats would not do because they are exposed to the open ocean.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I submit whether that is not an open request to the government for some aid to be given to the fishermen in the county of Lunenburg. I may say for the information of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) that when an item was up for discussion last year in connection with the same county, my hon. friend from Lunenburg asked this :
I hope the minister will expend that sum this year.
And the hon. member for Guysborough said, ' Strike it out.'
It ought to be struck out.

Well, I am not here to say whether it ought to be struck out or not. t am only pointing out that the hon. member for Guysborough, who is so anxious about the counties in the province he represents, when an item was up in the estimates for the county represented by an hon. gentleman on this side of the House, the hon. member for Guysborough so far forgot his interest in the fishermen for that county as to say ' Strike it out.' I might ask the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) why he wants it struck out ?
The hon. member is mistaken, I made no interruption.

I am just pointing out to the Finance Minister that my hon. friend from Lunenburg has not forgotten his duty. And perhaps the Minister of Finance will say why it is that that county has been overlooked ?

I did not make any charge of neglect against the hon. member for Lunenburg (Sir. Kaulbach). I stated that I was not aware, except as respects dredging, of any application that my hon. friend had made from his county. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Biain) now calls attention to something my hon. friend said a year ago. Well, I can only say that when these estimates were being prepared I sent to the Public Works Department and asked if there were any applications from Lunenburg, and I was informed there were none. I do not want to find fault with the hon. member for Lunenburg ; he has been here for seven months, and I think that if this matter was of such vital importance, he might have taken the trouble to place it before the department. However, I am not making any accusation against the member for Lunenburg, far from it. Since I am speaking on the subject, let me say that there is a great difference between the county of Lunenburg and some other counties, notably the county of Victoria, in respect to fishing. Lunenburg is a county in which the great mass of the fishermen are deep-sea fishermen, who go away in fine vessels. They are not so much concerned as the boat fishermen in the matter of small breakwaters and works of that character, and it might follow that the member for Lunenburg would not want works of this character at ail, though there is one particular place the hon. gentleman now speaks of. But there is that important difference. There is another difference. The county of Victoria has no railway, not a mile of railway, and no prospect of any. This county, thus isolated, is exposed to the ocean and there is no other county in the province which is at such disadvantage in regard to the facilities for travel and the means of communication. It is only by such aids as these that have been granted that the people of that county can really carry on their business as boat fishermen. There is a very important difference, and nobody knows it better than the hon. gentleman from Lunenburg. The fishermen of his county are of a different class, as respects the majority. There are some boat fishermen, but the great majority of the fishing population in the county of Lunenburg, and the most prosperous fishermen in Nova Scotia, are the deep-sea fishermen, whose condition is not exactly the same as that of the boat fishermen.

I beg slightly to differ from the Minister of Finance in one particular. From the border of the county of Queen's, which he represents, to the county of Halifax, there is one continuous line of habitations of fishermen who are dependent very largely upon shore fishing for their living. There is another class of fishermen, known as deep-sea fishermen, most of whom Mr. BLAIN.
live along the shore, and a large number of whom depend entirely upon that kind of fishing in the summer time. But as soon as spring and autumn come they are then dependent upon the shore fishing, and look to that largely for their living. This year they are compelled to look to it entirely in consequence of the failure of the deep-sea fishing. Now, with regard to the appeal for assistance, the Minister of Finance must know that it was only two months ago I said to him, when meeting him : ' You will not forget me in the estimates.' Well, I will not say a great deal about that. I do not want to make an appeal from day to day, and make myself appear ridiculous, and get an answer by way of a refusal, but I certainly, from the friendly remark that was made at that time, expected that I would see something in the estimates for the county of Lunenburg.

I would like to refer to the statement made by the hon. Minister of Finance in regard to the county of Victoria. I think he said that it extended from the gulf on one side to the Atlantic on the other. Is that correct ?

I saidi that Victoria had the sfea on two sides of it. Cape North is in the county of Victoria' and part of it in Inverness. Tbe county of Victoria is one of the most isolated counties in Nova Scotia, having no railways whatever. That was the point of my observation.
I would like to ask the hon. minister what kind of a structure he is going to have at Briton Cove for oats to land at ?
It is proposed to construct a wharf 200 feet long by 16 feet wide. It is to be built of both faced and round timber and to have ballasted cribwork.
What depth of water will there be at the end of the wharf ?
Four and a-half feet at low water.
What is tbe rise of the tide there ?
About four feet.
Is it intended specially for the accommodation of the lobsterpacking industry which has bejen erected there lately ?
No, there is the lobster factory, but there is quite a large number of people interested besides those engaged in the lobster factory.

You will pardon me, Mr. Chairman, if I refer to a matter which

is of very material importance to the interests of the shore fishermen as well as thfe deep-sea fishermen, and it is the menace offered by the dog-fish frequenting the waters of Nova Scotia in certain seasons of the ypar. This is a matter that should be looked into very carefully. I know that petitions have been circulated through the various counties in Nova Scotia-I am not. sure about the adjoining provinces-and forwarded to the department of Marine and Fisheries in the early part of this year. 1 am sorry that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Pr&fontaine) is not present. I would likje to know what has been done in that respect. Something ought to be done, because, during the past two years the dog-fish have Ween in such numbers that they have driven every other description of edible fish out of the water. X think the government might take the matter up and view it carefully in the interest of the country generally.
Does my hon. friend mean that they will take this wharf ?
No, I do not mjean, that, but if the hon. minister gives me the' hint and says that I should bring it up later,; I shall do so.
All right.
Is it intended that the boats shall go and land their lobsters or other fish on the pier and then seek shelter elsewhere ?
I do not understand my hon. friend's question.

In Prince Edward Island where we carry on such an industry I know gentlemen who built their factories on headlands 100 feet high, built their own accommodation, and *[DOT]did not come tD the government and ask them for any assistance. These gentlemen found that by building their factories on these headlands, as high as this building, and placing their gear there; to hoist the lobsters from the fishermen's1 boats, canning the lobsters and placing them on the market, that they could makle money; Now, in this case, hon. gentlemen opposite are asking that an establishment having ten boats, which has been opened at Briton Cove, shall have the assistance of this government to the extent of expending $4,000 for the building of this wharf. This is only the commencement of this expenditure. I protest against this because I am aware that a fisherman in Prince Edward Island has to carry on his business through his enterprise and energy with whatever little, capital he can put into it himself without receiving any government assistance. The
gentlemen to whom I have referred and who have without any assistance established a business there, have found it to be very' remunerative. They have carried it on for years without any assistance of this kind. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser) spoke particularly of fish. I am not going to speak altogether of fish. Hie spoke of the great fishing industry of Nova Scotia. It is a gx-eat industry, and we are all proud of it. But it is not all fish there.; If the hon. gentleman will look at the reports of a few days ago he will find that that province is about exporting to the old world one thousand barrels of apples, worth $4 per barrel. So that, when we arise here to speak of fishing matters, we are not speaking altogether of the resources of that great country from which we come. It is true that there may be some sectionalisin. Our hon. friends opposite want to make it appear that the province of Ontario is dw rectly oppos/ed to the interests of the maritime provinces. I claim that is not correct. I have found that in all my intercourse with my friends from Ontario and Quebec on this side of the House they have always been willing to do what is right and fair by the people of the maritime provinces witho'ut distinction, whether it was New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island. I think it is a very bad policy for our lion, friends opposite to endeavour to place that particular province against the lower provinces in this respect. We are onie people from the west to the east. We are endeavouring, as far as possible, to carry out the great object of confederation. There should be no rivalry between one part of the country and the other, and the man "who raises that question-I do not care whether it is on this side of the House or the other- is an enemy to his country and not deserv-i ing of any praise from any person.
Cow Bay Run-breakwater to protect outlet of harbour, $4,000.

This is a vote of $4,000 to make provision' for the construction of a breakwater at the outlet of Cow Bay Run, situated at the mouth of Halifax harbour. This will complete the work ?

The report of the engineer says it will.

Cheticamp wharf, $11,500.

This will complete the work ; the total cost is $15,000.

This is to form a harbour of refuge for fishermen in Pictou county. The estimated cost is $2,000.

The chief engineer tells me that it can be better done under the supervision of our local engineer. This vote will complete the work.

This is to complete payment on the contract. The total expenditure has been $5,500.
Donald's Head-repairs to breakwater, $3,000. The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. This is in Shelburne and Queen's. The estimated cost of the work is $3,000.
Duncan's Cove approach to wharf, $200.

No.

Yes.
East J-eddore wharf, $1,800.

Yes.

The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, Yes, the total cost is estimated at $1,800.

i

A great many of these small works are petitioned for either to the department direct or to the members. Y^e ask for a report from the engineer, and it is on that report, as a rule, that these estimates are made up.
Five Islands wharf

repairs, $700.

It is a very proper expenditure. There is a good wharf there, and it ought to be repaired. Have you had a report from the engineer ?

Finlay Point wharf. $2,000.

The total cost of the work is $16,400, and this is to pay for the balance of the work under contract. It is in Cumberland eounty.
When was this work commenced ?
The contract was let during the present calendar year ; a vote was taken in the main estimates and this is to complete it.
What will be the depth of the water at the end of the pier ?
I do not know what the average depth of the water is. It is said at the spring of the year to be 45 feet. I do not know what it is at low-water.
It is in the Straits of Northumberland.

This work is not on the Straits of Northumberland, but is at the head of the Bay of Pundy. At high tide tlie depth of the water is sometimes 50 feet, and at low tide it is probably 12 or 15 feet. This landing pier is for the accommodation not only of Fort Lawrence, but of the town of Amherst as well. It is 2* miles from that town. The manufacturers there have complained for many years that they have not had facilities for unloading materials brought from the United States, particularly southern pine. Then, there are shipments of apples from the lower part of the Bay of Pundy and other things brought to Amherst, for which there is at present no landing place.
Did tlie town of Amherst make any contribution towards the cost, or give a site ?

If I may be allowed to answer tlie question, I may say that the town of Amherst has contributed nothing. I do not think the site will cost anything, because it is to be built where the land is not valuable. I may say that the town of Amherst is a leading manufacturing town, and contributes largely to the revenue.
Has any work been done on the wharf so far ?

I expect so, as the contract was let in June.
tMr. BLAIN. What was the amount V

Fourteen thousand, eight hundred and
ninety-five dollars. It is estimated that this will complete the work.
Freeport-landing pier, $3,500.
- The MINISTER OP PDBLIC WORKS. This is in Digby county. It is to provide for the construction of a landing pier at Freeport, on the east side of the Grand Passage between Long island and Brier island. It will reach a depth of 10 feet at low water in ordinary spring tide.
Granite village-mooring pier, $1,000.
