Gabarouse-extension of breakwater, &c., $6,000.
Is that for the completion or the commencement of the work 1
This is for a continuation of a work that was under way. It is to be 80 feet long and 27 feet wide. This is the amount which the chief engineer estimates will complete the work now undertaken.
This is in the county of Cape Breton is it not ?
Yes.
Is this being done by day's work ?
Yes.
Why are these works being done by day's work ?

They ar not all being done by day's work. It is to be done by tender and contract, except works which the chief engineer reports, for reasons given, can be better and more economically done by our own engineers buying materials and employing men, such as repairs and improvements, for which specifications cannot be made and which, if done by contract, would cost a great deal more.	,
I can understand how the repairing of a wharf would be better done by day's work ; but where there is $6,000 for the extension of a pier-
I find that I was mistaken in regard to this work. It will be done by contract.
There was $3,500 voted for this work last year. Is it the policy of the department to have an engineer's report for a work before any money is voted for it V
In almost every case.
What was the vote of $3,500 for ?
There was an expenditure of $4,800 on this same breakwater, and $3,900 was spent on dredging at that point.
What is the call for this very great expenditure on this breakwater ?

I may say Gabarouse is the largest Ashing district in the county of Cape Breton. For twenty-five or thirty years the inhabitants of that place have requested successive governments to construct a breakwater. I have myself seen six large vessels smashed on the shore for want of this protection. Three or four years ago the Minister of Public Works visited the place and became impressed with the necessity of a beakwater. The representatives of Cape Breton county for the present and the future will not be satisfied unless larger appropriations are made for the work. This amount of $6,000 will perhaps be little more than sufficient to buy the creosoted timber which is necessary, and next year I shall ask the government to make a further vote to complete the work. It is an important work, and as long as I represent the county, I shall urge the government to make a sufficient appropriation to afford the necessary protection.
Might I ask the hon. gen-leman if there was a petition presented to the government for this work ?

I may tell the hon. gentleman that petitions were presented to the late government again and again, but they turned a deaf ear to them. Petitions were made for this extension to my colleague and myself on several occasions and to the government, and we were determined to have this work constructed.

I would like to know how the ear of the government is to be reached in connection with works of this kind. My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) has tried to get the attention of the government on behalf of his county but without avail. The Finance Minister has told us that petitions have been sent in from time to time for this work, how did these get to the ear of the government ? Of course, my hon. friend (Mr. Ivendall) made a little threat about next year. Here is an amount of $3,500 for last year, and $6,000 for this year, and the hon. gentleman representing the county (Mr. Kendall) has given notice that that is not nearly enough and that next year they shall come for a further amount. When will this cease ?
I am asking for a piece of work 80 feet long by 27 feet wide. If any further extension is required, it will be for the House to judge whether that will be granted.
What about the $3,500 ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC 'WORKS. There was a contract for $8,500, and $3,500 is for the approach.
$3,500 was asked last year to vote a breakwater there. What became of the money ?
That was for a part of the breakwater, 190 feet long, which was under contract. It was to complete the contract under way.
There is a further expenditure.
Yes, and it does not go far enough.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Has the hon. minister experimented in putting down some of these piers with cement instead of with timber as I suggested last year. By using cement, we would not have to spend so much money on repairs.

In some of the larger works, I have decided to use cement instead of timber. In some of the smaller works, I have asked the engineer to change from wood to cement when there is not too much difference in the cost.
Cement would last longer without repairs, would it not ?
If cement is well done, it lasts almost for ever.
And where you use creosote timber, you have to import it, whereas you can get the cement in our own country.
Yes.
Is this work intended to concentrate the water of the river in the main channel or is it built into the ocean ?
It is in the ocean.
What will be the depth of water inside the breakwater ?
Ten to fifteen feet.
That would give protection in local shipping.

Yes.
Glace Bay, N.S.-wharf, $15,000.

There was a prolonged discussion on this subject last session. I am asking $15,000, and the money will not be spent unless an agreement, such as was then discussed in a general way, be entered into by the company.

I think the point made was that the bay, once this wharf was constructed, should be the property of the Crown and that some arrange-

ment should be made with the coal company to that effect.
Yes.
Were any moneys collected at this wharf ?

The property is vested in the Dominion Coal Company, and the people have been asking for improvements which would cost a great deal of money. It was thought that some arrangement might be come to between the private owners and the department, which will be satisfactory and save a large expenditure.
Were no moneys collected at this wharf ?
The Dominion Coal Company are owners at present, and will collect the wharfage. The government have nothing to do with the wharfage.

But this company is asking for $25,000.
The MINISTER OB' FINANCE. No, it is the people of Glace Bay, and not the company, who are asking for this money. The company are indifferent. Glace Bay used to be a shipping point but the company constructed a line of railway and shipped their coal elsewhere and the harbour fell into disuse. In the meantime it has become the centre of a mining district, with a population of some 20,000 within a radius of three miles, and the people desire communication by water as well as by rail. The idea is that if the government will give something, the company will be induced to co-operate and the harbour may be opened and a public wharf established there.
Will the wharf belong to the public ?
That will have to be a matter of negotiation between (lie company and the government.
Then it is not a public wharf and will not be until some future arrangement is made.	-

It will have to be a public wharf, but the company might have some privileges over it in return for its contribution. The opening of a harbour and general improvements will cost a good deal more than $15,000. It will be a wharf in the general sense. But there will have to be an arrangement with the company.
The contention of the company was that they owned this harbour. That is to say, it is not a harbour at all until made so by the company.
The old Glace Bay Mining Company.

Originally it was not a harbour, but it was made so by one of these companies whose rights are now vested in the Dominion Coal Company. A company could not interfere with a navigable water but it might be possible that this company having itself created a navigable water would have absolute control of it. When this vote came up before us, the point was taken by myself that before the government expended a large sum of money for the benefit of the public in Glace Bay they should see to it that the public would actually have rights in the harbour. It would therefore be necessary to procure from that company some assignment or conveyance of it rights so that when the harbour should be once established and the wharf built, the public would have the same rights as if the harbour had been a navigable water in tiie first instance.
That is quite right.

I have here the Sydney ' Daily Post ' and in it I find an article in which it is stated that this matter has been the subject of negotiations carried on by a civic committee of which Mr. D. M. Burchell and Henry McDonald, of Glace Bay, were members. The item reads :
The supplementary estimates brought down in parliament contain an item of $15,000 for improvements of Glace Bay harbour. This with the $10,000 previously voted makes up the amount asked for by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, lessees of the Dominion Coal Company.
That would be $25,000 altogether, including the $10,000 in the original and the $15,000 now asked for. A letter is published in this paper from Mr. C. Shields, late manager of the company, to the committee above named, in which he says :

, March 9, 1903.
Gentlemen,-Replying to your favour of the 4th instant regarding Glace Bay harbour :-
As stated by me to your committee the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, lessees of the Dominion Coal Company, will build and repair its piers and wharfs at Glace Bay harbour, and also erect a coal shipping pier for the purpose of loading coal vessels coming to the port with produce or other freight and which desire a cargo of coal. It being understood, however, that we will not undertake to sell coal in order to find loading for such vessels, but will use them to move coal that we have sold as suits our convenience, or to sell them cargoes of coal if they desire it.
The above offer is made providing the government will grant the sum of $25,000 towards the repairs, and rebuilding the piers and wharfs

The opening of the harbour at Glace Bay has been an issue for at least four or five years. As has been stated, this harbour is the property of the Dominion Coal Company. A number of years ago the Dominion Coal Company abandoned that harbour as a port for shipping coal and the people of Glace Bay and the surrounding district have felt for many years that it would be to their interest to have this harbour reopened and to have the Dominion Coal Company induced to resume the shipment of coal from it. Negotiations were carried on for a number of years between the Dominion Coal Company and the town council of Glace Bay. The letter which the bon. gentleman has read was written by the late manager of the Dominion Coal Company to a committee of the town council of Glace Bay. who were conducting negotiations between the town and the company. In order that the harbour might become the property of the government it would be necessary in the first instance to purchase the harbour. I myself approached the Dominion Coal Company three or four years ago and conducted some correspondence with them ; at that time they stated that they would not sell the harbour. It was felt then by the committee, consisting of the. mayor of Glace Bay, who is familiar with the interests and requirements of the people of that neighbourhood, and other gentlemen equally interested in the welfare of the town, that the best solution of this question was that which Is set forth in the letter from the general manager of the coal company to the committee. That delegation was in Ottawa at one time. The gentlemen present being the mayor of Glace Mr. INGRAM.
Bay, Mr. Henry Macdonald, who was a member of the council, and Mr. N. J. Gillis, one of the members of the local legislature and a resident of Glace Bay. They discussed this matter with the members of the government and with my colleague and myself and we all concluded that the interests 6f Glace Bay would be very well served by the government contributing this $25,000 towards the reopening of the harbour. The company estimate that in order to open the harbour and make it a fit place for the shipment of coal an expenditure of at least $75,000 would be required. For my part I feel that the mayor of Glace Bay and those who were associated with him in these negotiations will take good care that the rights of the people of Glace Bay are fully protected. Personally I will see, so far as I am able to see, that all possible rights are secured to the people of Glace Bay on these wharfs proposed to be rebuilt by the Dominion Coal Company. They have gone into this matter and have represented to my colleague and myself that if the Dominion Coal Company undertake to reopen the harbour and resume shipping coal it will be decidedly in the interests of the people at Glace Bay and at the surrounding collieries. Those who are acquainted with the situation know very well that this is a most important work and feel that the plan proposed and agreed upon between the committee of the town council of Glace Bay and the Dominion Coal Company, if carried into effect, would be perfectly satisfactory and I am satisfied that it would be perfectly satisfactory to the government.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to mean that the people of this district prefer the arrangement as he has stated.	.

I state without any hesitation whatever that the general opinion in the district as represented by, the mayor and members of the delegation is overwhelmingly in favour of such an arrangement as I have indicated.
Is the entrance to this harbour on the property of the company, or is it public property 7
The entrance to the harbour is public property of course. It is on the shores of the Atlantic.
And is it properly protected so that the company could not monopolize the entrance to the harbour ?
There is no danger in the world of the company monopolizing the entrance, even if they wished to. The more trade comes to the harbour the better it is for the company.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman who represents the county why it was abandoned, why the original harbour was abandoned ?

It was abandoned when tbe property of tbe Glace Bay Mining Company, wlio were originally conducting tbe mining operations there, became tbe property of tbe Dominion Coal Company. In 1893 tbe coal properties in that region were consolidated, and as a result the Glace Bay Mining Company shipped its coal there. But tbe Dominion Coal Company constructed lines of railway between Louisburg and Sydney and concentrated as much as possible tbe shipping of its coal to Louisburg and Sydney.
Is there plenty of water V
Yes.
When this matter was up last year the acting minister stated they had abandoned it for lack of water.

It is not correct that they abandoned it for the sole reason that there was not sufficient water.
' They abandoned it ifor the reason I have stated.

There may have been a lack of water for .the larger class of vessels which were engaged in the coal trade. The Glace Bay Company conducted its operations on a modest scale, and their coal was handled with small vessels. The new enterprise undertook to employ heavier vessels, and for that reason they could not send their larger vessels into Glace Bay harbour. So, in a sense, it was due to lack of water for the larger vessels engaged in the coal trade.
The Minister of Finance said last year there was formerly a coal mine at Glace Bay, and after it was purchased by the new company they ceased shipping there, owing to lack of water.

That would mean lack of water for the larger vessels.
Mr, LEFURGEY. I would like to know if the government lias received any offer from the Dominion Coal Company as to the deepening of this harbour and the dredging and repairing of the wharf ?

No definite conclusion has been come to. As the member for Cape Breton Mi-. Johnston) has said, megotiattions have been going on, and it is assumed that a satisfactory arrangement could be made from a public standpoint if we had a vote of $25,000. The matter has been gone into fully and discussed on the floors of the House. The local people have offered to make arrangements for the improvements. Of course it is for the government to say whether these arrangements are satisfactory before they will agree to them.

I understand that the Dominion Coal Company own practically 413J
the whole harbour front there, and that there is a good deal of dissatisfaction among the residents of Glace Bay and vicinity as to the handling of these properties by the Dominion Coal Company. I also understand that the late general manager of the company, Mr. Shields, agreed or proposed that the company should dredge the harbour and fix up the wharfs if the government would give them $25,000 as a bonus. Now, Mr. Shields has left the company, and we have no guarantee that the Dominion Coal Company will dredge the harbour and repair the wharfs.
The hon. member will see that we submit this estimate provisionally. No part of this money will be spent unless a satisfactory arrangement is made.

Nothing should be done until some arrangement is made satisfactory to the people of that vicinity. I think, as I have said, that the proper way to deal with this question is to appropriate part of the harbour front for the people of Glace Bay. There is a population of 25,000 or 30,000 in that territory who want to use this harbour, and I do not think that a monopoly of it should be held by one large corporation, or that we should give them $25,000 to keep up that monopoly. I understand that when the harbour front was prepared they changed the road and took away part of the public highway in order to take in these rights.
Let me say one word more. I would like to say to my hon. friend that his informant is not up to date.
My informant comes from Glace Bay, and possibly knows as much about it as the hon. gentleman.

I know exactly where the hon. gentleman's information comes from. However, I want to say to the hon. gentleman that the successor of Mr. Shields, Mr. Duggan, has stated that he is prepared to carry out the arrangement entered into toy his predecessor in the office as manager of the Dominion Coal Company. Only a short time ago he was waited upon by the mayor, Mr. Burchell, and Mr. Macdonald, and others, in connection with this very matter, and Mayor Burchell and his associates received the assurance of Mr. Duggan that he was prepared to carry out every proposition submitted on behalf of his own company by Mr. Shields.
I do not think that this government should spend $25,000 upon the faith of any verbal statements by the manager of the Dominion Coal Company, however respectable he may be.

I would like the minister to tell the committee what he considers would be a proper arrangement to make with this company. We have had

some explanations, but still the affair appears to me mysterious. I would like to know from the minister what arrangements he thinks should be made with this company, so that the interests of the public might be protected, and that we might feel sure in voting this money that it was going for the benefit of the community and not of a corporation.

The matter is somewhat complicated. These people put a high value upon their property. On a previous occasion the House seemed to he favourable to making a contribution, provided it -could be done on terms that would be in the public interest.
Do we understand the minister to say that the negotiations that have -taken place were of a verbal character ?

There have been representations between the municipality and the company as I understand, and representations have been made to the government with regard to what the company were willing to do. I may say to -the committee that the company's interests there are very large. It will cost the Dominion an immense amount of money to provide the same facilities that the company offer to provide. If an arrangement can be come to between the company and the department by which the public interest will be secured, we will carry it out, if not this money will not be used.

That is not very satisfactory to this committee. The hon. gentleman is asking for $2-5,000 for an entirely new work. Now, we are asking if this is a verbal arrangement entered into between Glace Bay and the government ?
I have already said that there is no arrangement.
Then what is the object of the government in putting $25,000 into the estimates ?
So that if we can make a satisfactory arrangement we will have this money to carry out this work. If not, it will not be spent.

The minister is not frank with the committee. Surely these people came to the -government in order to induce them to put this $25,000 in the estimates. If they had a proposition to make to the government, either verbally or in writing, it should have been communicated to this committee. It is only fair we should know what the proposition is.

I could not state it half as well as the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has stated it to-day. I am sure he grasped it thoroughly. My hon. friend from Mr. COCHRANE
Cape Breton (Mr. Johnston) has explained in a general way the arrangement that is proposed to be made.

I may be thick headed enough not to understand it, and I do not believe that any lion, member on this side of the House can understand what the government anticipates in the shape of an expenditure for the dredging of this harbour. What obligation does the government undertake if we vote this $25,000, and what expenditure does the hon. minister anticipate that the government will be liable to make if this arrangement is carried out ? The hon. member -for Cape Breton says that an arrangement has been entered into between these parties.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) has misunderstood me. I did not say there was an arrangement entered into between the Dominion Coal Company and the government. What I did say was that the Dominion Coal Company had submitted a proposition to the town council of Glace Bay. That proposition, as embodied in a letter written by the general manager of the Dominion Coal Company, the hon. gentleman himself read a few moments ago. The hon. gentleman will find that the substance of the proposition is that the Dominion Coal Company propose to do certain work, provided the Dominion government make a grant of $25,000.
Is that an answer to the question I asked, if these people were satisfied with what the government were doing?

They are perfectly satisfied. I have no hesitation in saying that if the Dominion government carry out the proposal embodied in the letter of the Dominion Coal Company, the overwhelming majority of the people interested would be perfectly satisfied that the government had done their duty. As far as I am concerned, I feel that I can speak for the mayor of Glace Bay and for others in the council, when I say that they will take every possible means in their power to have secured to the people of Glace Bay the same rights in respect to this harbour as if the property were entirely theirs. That is my own position, it is the position of my colleagues and the position of the mayor of Glace Bay and those associated with him in this matter.
I do not understand that the company have an exclusive right to the harbour at all.
They own it. They constructed it.

They cannot own it. Even if it were an artificial harbour, the moment they construct it it is dedicated to the public. The public have a right to pay for the user of it a fair remuneration.

No company can erect a harbour on the sea coast and have it exclusively for their own purposes. They could no more do that than they could have a navigable river exclusively for their own purposes.

I understand that they procured these rights before confederation, but whether it was before or since, they could have procured these rights from the Crown at the time, whether by provincial or Dominion legislation. That is the position of affairs.
It could only be by Act of parliament. I do not understand how the provincial government would have the power to give over a harbour and the exclusive rights to it to an individual.

I think my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is quite right as far as navigable waters are concerned. There has been a decision that the Crown cannot grant any right that will interfere with navigation without the authority of un Act of parliament. It may be that there was in this instance such an Act of Nova Scotia, perhaps, before confederation. I do not know anything about that, but I understand that the company claims to have exclusive rights in that harbour, because they have practically made the harbour themselves. What I was insisting upon when an item in connection with this work was up for discussion was that the government, after spending $25,000, should be the owner -of the wharf. Further than that, I say that absolute rights should be conceded to the public in respect to this harbour.

It was in view of the discussion between my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that I undertook to bring down this vote, and it, was with the intention of carrying -out the arrangement based upon the remarks made at that time.

This is a question that must have been considered for some time, and yet we are now in the position that we have this supplementary estimate brought down asking for this increased sum of money. I have complained all along that one of the abuses that has been permitted In this House is that the government come down and ask for a sum to be placed in the estimates without informing parliament what the proposition is and what obligation the expenditure of the money will impose upon the government. The time of this House has been taken up session after session with the consideration of such votes as this. I had hoped at the early part of the session, when the hon. minister assured us that if any new work was to be undertaken, tfor which a large sum of money was to be asked, he would have full and ample Information laid before the House showing
the purpose to which the money was to be devoted. We are now told that unless there is a satisfactory arrangement entered into the money will not be spent. Lest this work should turn out a sink-hole for the expenditure of public money, it is time that we should pause before we proceed with it any further. Let us have the information, let us know what the probable cost of dredging this harbour is going to be. The government must agree to the arrangement before they can meet the views of the coal company, because the coal company say that the government must dredge out the harbour. They say that they are willing to dredge out between the piers inside the harbour. Before entering into an arrangement of that kind, we should know how much it would cost. It may require that a sum of money shall be expended every year upon the dredging of that harbour, or it may be that it will only be necessary to dredge the harbour once in two or five years. But if it is necessary that the dredging shall be done year after year, the money of the country will be wasted.

The harbour of Port Hood, some 50 or 60 years ago, was one of the best harbours in eastern Nova Scotia, and was the home of the American fishing fleet, when there was a treaty of reciprocity between the United States and Canada. On many occasions about 300 sail would take shelter in Port Hood harbour, coming in from the storms of the gulf of St. Lawrence. About

sixty or seventy years ago Smith's Island which is about a mile from the coast, was connected with the mainland by a narrow sandy beach, including a sheet of water about two miles long and a mile wide, constituting the harbour of Port Hood. At that time it was an excellent harbour of refuge. But this narrow beach was at first broken up slightly by the waves, and a small channel was formed through it, which has continued from that day to this, though the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence beating in through it every year since have made it considerably wider. During that time the government of Nova Scotia had this wharf, upon which repairs are now to be made, built inside the harbour. At the time of confederation the Dominion government took over the wharf and made repairs and extensions to it. But owing to the breach in the beach to which I have referred, the sand began to pour in along the coast and right up against the government wharf, rendering a great portion of the harbour useless. I may say that where about sixty years ago the admiralty chart showed forty or forty-five feet of water in Port Hood harbour, there is not to-day over six or seven feet. That portion of the harbour which is exposed to the northwest wind is especially filling up badly with sand, Some years ago a coal mining company took hold of the coal areas just at the entrance to this harbour, within 300 or 400 yards of the water's edge. For about twenty years very little was done in developing this property. But about six or seven years ago, certain gentlemen from the cities of Toronto, Montreal and Halifax, took hold of this coal property, and built a shipping pier along the southern portion of this harbour, at an expense to the company of about $60,000. But it was found by experience that year after year, the northern entrance being open, the sand was pouring in and was not only injuring the shipping facilities around the government wharf, but was also reaching the company's pier at the southern entrance to the harbour. This company, then, in common with the public, are pressing upon the government the importance of having this northern entrance closed, if not altogether, at least partially in the meantime, and a sufficiently long pier built from the shore to keep out the sand, for a. number of years at least. It is supposed by the local engineer, and it is also the opinion of the chief engineer, that as the pier is extended out the sand will bank up against it, and thus make it perfectly safe to "have this entrance closed with work composed of brushwood and stone. I may say that the importance of this harbour was considered to be so great in the year 1878 that Sir Charles Tupper spoke of it in this House in the following words :
